readerTitle: Why a higher price can bring more customers
caseNote: 일화 (Cialdini의 보석 가게) + 실제 연구 (Waber 외 2008, 진통제 가격 실험) + 가상 적용 (주택 점검, 사내 교육팀)
insight: 고객이 품질을 직접 판단하기 어려울 때 가격은 비용이 아니라 정보가 된다. 그래서 너무 낮은 가격은 수요를 줄일 수 있다.
misconception: 가격을 내리면 언제나 더 많은 고객이 온다. 수요 곡선은 항상 아래로 기운다.

sources.text: Cialdini, R. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. 터키석 보석 일화
Waber, R. L., Shiv, B., Carmon, Z., & Ariely, D. (2008). Commercial features of placebo and therapeutic efficacy. JAMA, 299(9), 1016–1017.
주택 점검과 사내 교육팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Cialdini 일화: 애리조나의 보석 가게, 주인이 '× ½' 메모를 남겼는데 직원이 '× 2'로 읽었고 그 뒤 물건이 다 팔렸다는 내용. 저자가 지인에게 들은 이야기로 소개된 것이므로 카드에 일화로 표시했습니다. 세부 묘사는 원문과 다시 대조하세요.
Waber 외(2008): 참가자 82명, 전기 자극 통증, 같은 위약을 정가 $2.50 또는 할인가 $0.10로 소개. 통증 감소 보고 약 85% 대 61%. 원문 수치(85.4%, 61.0%)를 게시 전에 확인하세요.
주택 점검 가격($250, 지역 평균 약 $400)은 가상 수치입니다. 실제 시장 시세를 나타내지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why a higher price can bring more customers
body: A story Robert Cialdini tells in his book *Influence*: a jewelry shop couldn't sell a case of turquoise pieces. Before a trip, the owner left a note: "Everything in this case, price × ½."
An employee misread it as × 2. The pieces reportedly sold out, at double the price. It's an anecdote, but the pattern behind it is real.

image.label: A jewelry display case with a handwritten price note
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 유리 진열장 안의 청록색 보석들, 그 위에 손글씨 메모 "× ½". 메모의 '½'이 '2'처럼 번져 보이게. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your home inspections aren't booking.
body: You've started a home inspection business. Buyers hire you once, before the biggest purchase of their lives. You charge $250. Most local inspectors charge around $400.
Bookings are slow. What do you try first?

options.text: Drop to $199 to stand out even more
options.feedback: Cheaper usually wins. But a buyer who can't judge an inspection may read $199 as "this one cuts corners" and keep scrolling.

options.text: Raise to about $400 and spell out what's checked
options.feedback: You give up the bargain angle and gain a price that says "serious professional." For a rare, high-stakes job, that's often what buyers are looking for.

options.text: Keep $250 and spend more on ads
options.feedback: More people will see you. But if the price itself is making them doubt you, more views mean more doubt.

cards.title: The same pill worked better at $2.50.
body: In a 2008 study, researchers gave volunteers mild electric shocks, then a "new painkiller." It was a sugar pill.
Half were told it cost $2.50 a dose. Half were told it was discounted to 10 cents. About **85%** of the full-price group reported less pain, against about 61% of the discount group.
Same pill. The price changed what people expected, and even what they felt.

cards.title: Price as a signal of quality
body: Normally, a higher price means fewer buyers. But when customers **can't judge quality** before buying, they use price as a clue. A low price can say "something's wrong." A higher one can say "this is the good one."
When that happens, raising the price can raise demand, at least up to a point. It doesn't break the usual rule. It adds information the customer was missing.

image.label: A demand line that bends upward at low prices
image.brief: 간단한 그래프. 가로축 'Price', 세로축 'Customers'. 아주 낮은 가격 구간에서는 가격이 오를수록 고객이 늘다가, 어느 지점을 지나면 다시 줄어드는 완만한 언덕 모양. 언덕 왼쪽 비탈에 "Too cheap to trust" 라벨.

cards.title: Look for these conditions.
body: The effect is strongest when several of these are true:
list: **Quality is hidden:** a lawyer, a contractor, a surgeon, a wine
**Mistakes are costly:** a bad choice hurts more than the price saved
**Purchases are rare:** no past experience to compare
**The price is seen by others:** watches, bags, and gifts, where a high price is part of the point
cards.callout: Cheap toothpaste doesn't need to look expensive. A wedding photographer might.
cards.softwareNote: Business software often hits this. A buyer choosing a security or payroll tool for a whole company may skip the $9 option because it looks like a toy, and shortlist the one priced like a serious vendor.

cards.title: The signal fades when quality becomes visible.
body: Price stands in for information. Once customers can try, compare or read honest reviews, they judge the product directly, and the usual rule comes back.
A high price also sets a promise. If the work doesn't match it, you get one sale and a bad review. And every market has a ceiling: past some point, a higher price loses customers again.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You run the in-house training team at a large firm. Your negotiation workshop is free to every department. Sign-ups are low, and managers keep hiring an outside trainer for a similar course at a high fee.

options.text: Send more reminder emails about the free workshop
options.feedback: Cheap and easy, and some will come. But it doesn't touch the reason managers trust the outside course more.

options.text: Charge departments a real internal fee, limit seats, and share results from past groups
options.feedback: A fee and limited seats tell managers this is worth budget, and results give them proof. You risk some sign-ups at first if the course can't back up the price.

options.text: Cut the workshop to half a day to make it easier to attend
options.feedback: It lowers the time "price," but shorter and free can look even less valuable next to the outside trainer.

cards.title: When quality is hard to see, price tells the story.
body: If customers can't judge your work before buying, a low price may be costing you trust, not winning you sales.
**Try it today:** ask three recent customers how they judged you before hiring you. If none of them could, check what your price was saying.
